theory.what: IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses (vs IPv4's 32-bit), providing virtually unlimited addresses. Format: eight groups of four hex digits separated by colons.
theory.why: IPv4 addresses are exhausted. IPv6 is the future of networking — already used by major providers. Understanding IPv6 is increasingly required for network engineers.
theory.how:
IPv6 address: 2001:0db8:85a3:0000:0000:8a2e:0370:7334
Shortened: 2001:db8:85a3::8a2e:370:7334

Types: Global Unicast (public), Link-Local (fe80::), Multicast (ff00::)
No broadcast in IPv6 — uses multicast instead.
No NAT needed — every device gets a public address.
theory.when: IPv6 is used alongside IPv4 (dual-stack) in most modern networks. Required for: mobile networks, IoT, and future-proofing.
theory.configuration:
# Linux
ip -6 addr add 2001:db8::1/64 dev eth0
ip -6 route add default via 2001:db8::ffff

# Cisco
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ipv6 address 2001:db8::1/64
 ipv6 enable

theory.what: HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) is the foundation of web communication. HTTPS adds TLS encryption for security. Both use TCP port 80 (HTTP) and 443 (HTTPS).
theory.why: HTTP/HTTPS is the most common application protocol. Understanding it is essential for web troubleshooting, security (HTTPS enforcement), and application delivery.
theory.how:
HTTP request/response:
1. Client sends request (GET /page HTTP/1.1)
2. Server processes request
3. Server sends response (HTTP/1.1 200 OK + body)

Methods: GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, PATCH
Status codes: 2xx (success), 3xx (redirect), 4xx (client error), 5xx (server error)

HTTPS = HTTP + TLS (encryption + certificate verification).
theory.when: Every web application uses HTTP/HTTPS. Troubleshoot when: pages don't load, certificate errors, redirect loops, or slow page loads.
theory.configuration:
# Test HTTP
curl -v http://example.com
curl -I https://example.com  # Headers only

# Check certificate
openssl s_client -connect example.com:443

theory.what: SSH provides encrypted remote access to network devices and servers. It replaces insecure Telnet with strong encryption, authentication, and integrity checking.
theory.why: SSH is how you manage every Linux server and network device. Understanding SSH keys, tunneling, and configuration is essential for any IT professional.
theory.how:
SSH uses public-key cryptography:
1. Client connects to server (port 22)
2. Server presents host key (verify fingerprint)
3. Key exchange (Diffie-Hellman)
4. Authentication (password or public key)
5. Encrypted session established

Features: Remote shell, file transfer (SCP/SFTP), port forwarding, X11 forwarding.
theory.when: Use SSH for: all remote management, file transfers, tunneling, and any time you need encrypted remote access.
theory.configuration:
# Generate SSH key
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C 'user@host'

# Copy key to server
ssh-copy-id user@server

# SSH config (~/.ssh/config)
Host myserver
  HostName 192.168.1.10
  User admin
  IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

theory.what: FTP transfers files over the network (insecure, plaintext). SFTP and SCP provide encrypted file transfer over SSH.
theory.why: File transfer is a basic network operation. Understanding the security differences between FTP (insecure) and SFTP/SCP (encrypted) is important for secure operations.
theory.how:
FTP: Uses TCP ports 20 (data) and 21 (control). Plaintext — passwords visible on network.
SFTP: File transfer over SSH (port 22). Encrypted.
SCP: Secure copy over SSH. Simple but less features than SFTP.

Always prefer SFTP/SCP over FTP in production.
theory.when: Use SFTP/SCP for all file transfers. Only use FTP for legacy systems that don't support alternatives. Never use FTP for sensitive data.
theory.configuration:
# SCP
scp file.txt user@server:/path/
scp -r directory/ user@server:/path/

# SFTP
sftp user@server
sftp> put localfile.txt
sftp> get remotefile.txt
troubleshooting: FTP passive mode issues with NAT

theory.what: NTP synchronizes clocks across network devices. Accurate time is critical for logging, authentication (Kerberos), certificates, and forensics.
theory.why: If device clocks are wrong: logs are useless for correlation, Kerberos auth fails (5-min tolerance), certificates appear expired, and forensic timelines are unreliable.
theory.how:
NTP uses UDP port 123. Stratum hierarchy:
- Stratum 0: Atomic clocks, GPS
- Stratum 1: Directly connected to Stratum 0
- Stratum 2: Syncs from Stratum 1
- Stratum 3+: Each level syncs from above

NTP adjusts clock gradually (slew) rather than jumping.
theory.when: Configure NTP on EVERY network device and server. Use at least 2 NTP sources for redundancy. Critical for: SIEM, Kerberos, PKI, compliance.
theory.configuration:
# Cisco
ntp server 10.0.0.5
ntp server 10.0.0.6

# Linux (chrony)
server 0.pool.ntp.org iburst
server 1.pool.ntp.org iburst

# Verify
show ntp status
chronyc tracking
